LACTATION ACCOMMODATION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

LACTATION ACCOMMODATION POLICY STATEMENT
Acme, Inc. maintains this Lactation Accommodation Information Sheet to describe, for Jordan Lee's reference, the break time and location practices Acme, Inc. makes available to employees who are expressing breast milk, and the process by which an employee may request lactation accommodation. This is a statement of Acme, Inc.'s practice; it does not itself waive, expand, or limit any right or obligation that may exist under applicable law, and Jordan Lee may direct any request for lactation accommodation, or any question about this policy, to Acme, Inc.'s designated contact for such requests.

THE BREAK TIME DUTY AND ITS RELATIONSHIP TO PAID REST BREAKS
California law requires Acme, Inc., as an employer, to provide Jordan Lee a reasonable amount of break time to express breast milk for Jordan Lee's infant child each time Jordan Lee has need to do so. This break time must, if possible, run concurrently with any break time already provided to Jordan Lee, such as an existing paid rest period. Break time that does not run concurrently with the rest time otherwise authorized for Jordan Lee under the applicable Industrial Welfare Commission wage order is unpaid.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Every employer, including the state and any political subdivision, shall provide a reasonable amount of break time to accommodate an employee desiring to express breast milk for the employee’s infant child each time the employee has need to express milk. The break time shall, if possible, run concurrently with any break time already provided to the employee. Break time for an employee that does not run concurrently with the rest time authorized for the employee by the applicable wage order of the Industrial Welfare Commission shall be unpaid."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1030, Cal. Lab. Code § 1030 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1030.)
  Known gap: This is California's statute (Cal. Lab. Code § 1030), offered as documented evidence of what that provision says — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee. Federal law provides a separate, less detailed break-time requirement for nursing employees (29 U.S.C. § 218d, the PUMP Act), and most other states have no comparable statute. This is a single, self-contained statutory section; no additional independent source was located for this specific text.

THE CORE LACTATION LOCATION REQUIREMENT
California law requires Acme, Inc., as an employer, to provide Jordan Lee the use of a room or other location to express milk in private; this may include the place where Jordan Lee normally works if that place otherwise meets the statutory requirements. The location must not be a bathroom, and it must be in close proximity to Jordan Lee's work area, shielded from view, and free from intrusion while Jordan Lee is expressing milk.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "An employer shall provide an employee with the use of a room or other location for the employee to express milk in private. The room or location may include the place where the employee normally works if it otherwise meets the requirements of this section. (b) A lactation room or location shall not be a bathroom and shall be in close proximity to the employee’s work area, shielded from view, and free from intrusion while the employee is expressing milk."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1031(a)-(b), Cal. Lab. Code § 1031, subds. (a)-(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1031.)
  Known gap: This is California's statute (Cal. Lab. Code § 1031, subds. (a)-(b)), offered as documented evidence of what that provision says — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee. Federal law's parallel provision (29 U.S.C. § 218d) similarly requires a private, non-bathroom space, but California's statute is more detailed. This clause and the following one (on the location's specific features) are drawn from subdivisions of the same statutory section, not independent sources of each other; the exemption clause covering fewer-than-50-employee employers (§ 1031(i)) is likewise part of this same section.

REQUIRED FEATURES OF THE LACTATION LOCATION
California law requires that the lactation location Acme, Inc. provides to Jordan Lee be safe, clean, and free of hazardous materials; contain a surface to place a breast pump and personal items; contain a place to sit; and have access to electricity or an alternative such as an extension cord or charging station needed to operate a breast pump. California law separately requires Acme, Inc. to provide access to a sink with running water and a refrigerator suitable for storing milk in close proximity to Jordan Lee's workspace, or, if a refrigerator cannot be provided, another suitable cooling device such as an employer-provided cooler.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A lactation room or location shall comply with all of the following requirements: (1) Be safe, clean, and free of hazardous materials, as defined in Section 6382. (2) Contain a surface to place a breast pump and personal items. (3) Contain a place to sit. (4) Have access to electricity or alternative devices, including, but not limited to, extension cords or charging stations, needed to operate an electric or battery-powered breast pump. (d) The employer shall provide access to a sink with running water and a refrigerator suitable for storing milk in close proximity to the employee’s workspace. If a refrigerator cannot be provided, an employer may provide another cooling device suitable for storing milk, such as an employer-provided cooler."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1031(c)-(d), Cal. Lab. Code § 1031, subds. (c)-(d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1031.)
  Known gap: This is California's statute (Cal. Lab. Code § 1031, subds. (c)-(d)), offered as documented evidence of what that provision says — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee. This level of itemized detail (surface, seating, electricity, sink, refrigeration) goes beyond the federal PUMP Act's more general private-space requirement. This clause is drawn from the same statutory section as the two other § 1031 clauses in this document (location duty; small-employer exemption), not an independent source of either.

THE "SERIOUSLY DISRUPT OPERATIONS" EXEMPTION FROM THE BREAK TIME DUTY
California law provides that an employer is not required to provide break time under this chapter if doing so would seriously disrupt the employer's operations. This exemption applies to the break-time duty and is not, by its terms, limited to employers below a particular size.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "An employer is not required to provide break time under this chapter if to do so would seriously disrupt the operations of the employer."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1032, Cal. Lab. Code § 1032 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1032.)
  Known gap: This is California's statute (Cal. Lab. Code § 1032), offered as documented evidence of what that provision says — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer, nor an assessment of whether any particular employer's operations would in fact be seriously disrupted. This provision is easily confused with the separate, differently-worded exemption in § 1031(i) (covered in a companion clause in this document), which applies only to the location requirements and only for employers with fewer than 50 employees; § 1032's "seriously disrupt operations" standard, by contrast, applies to the break-time duty of § 1030 and contains no employee-count threshold. This is a single, self-contained statutory section unchanged since its original 2001 enactment; no additional independent source was located for this specific text.

THE FEWER-THAN-50-EMPLOYEES UNDUE HARDSHIP EXEMPTION FROM LOCATION REQUIREMENTS
California law provides that an employer with fewer than 50 employees may be exempt from a requirement of the lactation-location statute if it can demonstrate that the requirement would impose an undue hardship, by causing the employer significant difficulty or expense, when considered in relation to the size, financial resources, nature, or structure of the employer's business. Where an employer with fewer than 50 employees demonstrates that providing a room or other location other than a bathroom would impose such undue hardship, that employer is still required to make reasonable efforts to provide the use of a room or other location, other than a toilet stall, in close proximity to the employee's work area, for the employee to express milk in private.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "An employer that employs fewer than 50 employees may be exempt from a requirement of this section if it can demonstrate that a requirement would impose an undue hardship by causing the employer significant difficulty or expense when considered in relation to the size, financial resources, nature, or structure of the employer’s business. If that employer can demonstrate that the requirement to provide an employee with the use of a room or other location, other than a bathroom, would impose such undue hardship, the employer shall make reasonable efforts to provide the employee with the use of a room or other location, other than a toilet stall, in close proximity to the employee’s work area, for the employee to express milk in private."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1031(i), Cal. Lab. Code § 1031, subd. (i) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1031.)
  Known gap: This is California's statute (Cal. Lab. Code § 1031(i)), offered as documented evidence of what that provision says — not an assessment of whether any particular employer qualifies for the exemption or has fewer than 50 employees. This exemption applies specifically to the location requirements of § 1031; it is a distinct provision from the separately worded, employer-size-neutral "seriously disrupt operations" exemption from the break-time duty in § 1032 (covered in a companion clause in this document) and should not be conflated with it. This clause is drawn from the same statutory section (§ 1031) as the two other location-requirement clauses in this document, not an independent source of either.

THE WRITTEN LACTATION ACCOMMODATION POLICY REQUIREMENT
California law requires an employer to develop and implement a policy regarding lactation accommodation that includes a statement about an employee's right to request lactation accommodation, the process by which an employee makes that request, the employer's obligation to respond to the request, and a statement about the employee's right to file a complaint with the Labor Commissioner for a violation of this chapter. The employer must include this policy in an employee handbook or set of policies made available to employees, and must distribute the policy to new employees upon hiring and to any employee who inquires about or requests parental leave. If an employer cannot provide break time or a location that complies with the policy, the employer must provide a written response to the employee.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "An employer shall develop and implement a policy regarding lactation accommodation that includes the following: (1) A statement about an employee’s right to request lactation accommodation. (2) The process by which the employee makes the request described in paragraph (1). (3) An employer’s obligation to respond to the request described in paragraph (1) as outlined in subdivision (d). (4) A statement about an employee’s right to file a complaint with the Labor Commissioner for any violation of a right under this chapter. (b) The employer shall include the policy described in subdivision (a) in an employee handbook or set of policies that the employer makes available to employees. (c) The employer shall distribute the policy described in subdivision (a) to new employees upon hiring and when an employee makes an inquiry about or requests parental leave. (d) If an employer cannot provide break time or a location that complies with the policy described in subdivision (a), the employer shall provide a written response to the employee."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1034, Cal. Lab. Code § 1034 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1034.)
  Known gap: This is California's statute (Cal. Lab. Code § 1034), offered as documented evidence of what that provision says. This requirement was added effective January 1, 2020 by SB 142 (Stats. 2019, Ch. 720); it did not exist in the statute's original 2001 form. This is a single, self-contained statutory section; no additional independent source was located for this specific text.

ENFORCEMENT, ANTI-RETALIATION PROTECTION, AND CIVIL PENALTIES
California law treats the denial of reasonable break time or adequate space to express milk as a failure to comply with Labor Code Section 226.7, and an aggrieved employee may file a complaint with the Labor Commissioner under Section 98. Separately, an employer may not discharge, discriminate, or retaliate against an employee for exercising or attempting to exercise a right protected under this chapter, and an aggrieved employee may file a retaliation complaint with the Labor Commissioner under Section 98.7. An employee may also report a violation to the Labor Commissioner's field enforcement unit; if the Labor Commissioner finds a violation after inspection or investigation, the Labor Commissioner may issue a citation and impose a civil penalty of $100 for each day an employee is denied reasonable break time or adequate space, using the same procedures that apply to citations under Section 1197.1. Violations of this chapter are not misdemeanors under the Labor Code.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The denial of reasonable break time or adequate space to express milk in accordance with this chapter shall be deemed a failure to comply for purposes of Section 226.7. An aggrieved employee may file a complaint under this subdivision with the Labor Commissioner pursuant to Section 98. (b) An employer shall not discharge, or in any other manner discriminate or retaliate against, an employee for exercising or attempting to exercise any right protected under this chapter. This subdivision is not intended to limit or expand an employee’s rights pursuant to Section 98.6. An aggrieved employee may file a complaint under this subdivision with the Labor Commissioner pursuant to Section 98.7. (c) An employee may report a violation of this chapter to the Labor Commissioner’s field enforcement unit. If, upon inspection or investigation, the Labor Commissioner determines that a violation of this chapter has occurred, the Labor Commissioner may issue a citation and may impose a civil penalty in the amount of one hundred dollars ($100) for each day that an employee is denied reasonable break time or adequate space to express milk in violation of this chapter. The procedures for issuing, contesting, and enforcing judgments for citations or civil penalties issued by the Labor Commissioner for violations of this chapter shall be the same as those set forth in Section 1197.1. (d) Notwithstanding any other provision of this code, violations of this chapter shall not be misdemeanors under this code."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1033, Cal. Lab. Code § 1033 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1033.)
  Known gap: This is California's statute (Cal. Lab. Code § 1033), offered as documented evidence of what that provision says — not an assessment of whether any particular denial or dispute amounts to a violation. Because § 1033(a) deems a denial of break time or space a failure to comply with the separate meal-and-rest-period statute (§ 226.7), the practical remedies available for a lactation-accommodation violation may overlap with meal/rest-break remedies described elsewhere in this document; that cross-reference is stated by the statute itself, not inferred here. This is a single, self-contained statutory section; no additional independent source was located for this specific text.

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT
By signing below, Jordan Lee acknowledges having received and reviewed a copy of this Lactation Accommodation Information Sheet.
